name: The Paradox of Thrift
statement: If everyone saves more at once in a slump, incomes fall and total saving may not rise at all.
statementAccent: incomes fall and total saving may not rise at all
meaning: The paradox of thrift, also called the paradox of saving, is a proposition in economics popularised by John Maynard Keynes: if everyone tries to save more during an economic downturn, aggregate demand falls, which lowers total output and incomes, and can ultimately reduce total saving in the economy rather than increase it. What is prudent for an individual, saving more, can be harmful when everyone does it at once. Keynes formalised the idea in his 1936 General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, and it has earlier antecedents, including Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees. The paradox is a leading example of the fallacy of composition, the error of assuming that what is true for one part must be true for the whole. It applies chiefly in a demand-deficient recession, below full employment, and it is contested by economists who argue that at full employment increased saving simply funds investment.
mechanism: The paradox turns on the fact that one person's spending is another person's income. If a single household cuts consumption to save more, its saving rises and the economy is barely affected. But if all households do so simultaneously during a slump, businesses see sales fall, so they cut production and lay off workers, and incomes drop across the economy. With lower incomes, households cannot save as much as they intended, so aggregate saving does not rise, and may fall, while output contracts. This is the fallacy of composition at work: the attempt to save more, generalised, defeats itself by shrinking the incomes out of which saving comes. The multiplier amplifies the process, as each round of reduced spending lowers income and triggers further cuts. The paradox holds when the economy has idle resources and is constrained by demand; at full employment, the classical view is that extra saving lowers interest rates and is channelled into investment, so the self-defeating dynamic does not arise.

examples.text: When all households cut spending to save, businesses lose sales, incomes fall, and people end up unable to save as much as they intended.
What is prudent for one saver becomes harmful when everyone saves at once, since the collective attempt shrinks the incomes saving depends on.
The paradox is invoked against government belt-tightening in a recession, arguing that collective thrift can deepen a demand shortfall.

variants.name: The paradox of deleveraging
variants.text: A related dynamic in which everyone trying to pay down debt at once depresses demand and incomes, making deleveraging harder for all.

variants.name: The loanable-funds objection
variants.text: The classical counterargument that increased saving lowers interest rates and funds investment, so the paradox fails at full employment.

whyItMatters: The paradox of thrift is a central proposition of Keynesian macroeconomics, illustrating how individually sensible behaviour can be collectively harmful and why economies can get stuck in downturns. It is a vivid demonstration of the fallacy of composition and of the interdependence of spending and income, showing that during a demand-deficient recession a general rush to save can shrink output and defeat itself. The idea underlies the case against austerity in slumps and the argument for fiscal stimulus, since if households and firms all retrench, government spending may be needed to sustain demand and prevent a deeper contraction. It connects to related dynamics like the paradox of deleveraging and to the multiplier. Because it is also contested, with classical economists arguing that saving funds investment, the paradox of thrift sits at the heart of long-running debates about how economies behave in recessions and how policy should respond.

working.text: suppose all households cut consumption to increase saving during a downturn with idle resources.
note that lower spending means lower sales, so firms cut output and jobs, and incomes drop across the economy.
recognise that with lower incomes, households cannot save as intended, so total saving stalls or falls while output contracts.

limits: The paradox of thrift applies mainly in a demand-deficient recession, when the economy is below full employment with idle resources; it is not a general law of saving. At full employment, the classical and loanable-funds view holds that increased saving lowers interest rates and is channelled into productive investment, so more saving need not reduce output, and the paradox does not arise. Critics also note that saving is essential for long-run growth, so the paradox concerns short-run demand management, not the value of thrift over time. Whether and when the paradox binds depends on the state of the economy, the responsiveness of investment to interest rates, and monetary conditions. So it is a powerful and influential proposition within Keynesian conditions rather than a universal truth about saving.
misreadings: The paradox does not say saving is bad in general; it concerns a specific situation, a demand-deficient recession, in which a simultaneous rush to save can be self-defeating. It is not a claim that individual thrift is imprudent, only that generalising it in a slump lowers incomes and total saving, the fallacy of composition. And it is contested rather than universal: at full employment the classical view holds saving funds investment, so treating the paradox as always true, or as condemning thrift outright, misreads a proposition bounded by recessionary conditions.
origin: Popularised by John Maynard Keynes in his 1936 General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, with antecedents such as Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees; a central example of the fallacy of composition in Keynesian macroeconomics.
